newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Bangladesh says many Burma refugees must go -UNHCR.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh says many Burma refugees must go -UNHCR.

text.p: Bangladesh is insisting that around one-third of 21,000 Burmese Moslems left in the country from a flood of immigrants in the early 1990s must go home, the United Nations refugee agency UNHCR said on Friday.
Spokeswoman Pam O'Toole told a news briefing Bangladeshi officials had agreed that sick refugees should not have been forcibly returned to Burma in two repatriation operations earlier this week.
They also agreed that the UNHCR should be allowed to restore medical screening of those going back and allow people unfit to travel to stay behind until they recovered.
"However, Bangladesh continued to maintain during these meetings that those cleared for return must go," she added.

Some 7,500 of the Moslem Rohingyas have been accepted as Burmese citizens by the authorities in Rangoon and cleared for return. The others are either still having identities checked or have been rejected by Burma.
Most have been in Bangladesh at camps near the border since 250,000 crossed over in 1991-92, but some have arrived more recently.
The others have all returned in a repatriation process supervised by the UNHCR, which has some 20 expatriate staff working with the returnees in Burma's Arakan province.
Bangladesh, one of the world's poorest countries, insists that the refugees are economic migrants but leaders of the Rohingyas say they have fled political persecution by Burma's military rulers.

O'Toole said on Friday a "tense standoff" continued between the refugees and police in two camps near Cox's Bazar in south-east Bangladesh with all of the Moslems refusing food rations offered by the U.N. agency.

"Some of the refugees say they will never return to Myanmar (Burma) while it is under military rule. A few of the more radical demonstrators told officials they would 'fight to the death' rather than be sent back," she added.
In one of the camps, Kutupalong, Reuter correspondent Nizam Ahmed reported on Thursday that hundreds were demonstrating and threatening violence and suicide to prevent repatriation.

"It's better to die here than in Burma where persecution is commonplace," he quoted one refugee, Moqbul Ahmed who fled to Bangladesh years ago from a small township in Burma's Moslem-majority Arakan province, as saying.
"We don't want to go back to labour camps (in Burma), let our sisters and daughters be molested by soldiers and live a dreadful life," he added.
Hyatuz Zahan, a 55-year-old woman refugee, gave similar accounts. "Only a hell awaits us there," she said when asked if she would be willing to return.
"We will prevent any move to send us back. We will resist it by sacrificing our lives if necessary," she added.
Earlier on Thursday, Bangladesh postponed the repatriation of 200 refugees following protests over the earlier expulsions of 399 others on Sunday and Tuesday.
It was not known when repatriation would resume.
The deportations earlier this week sparked rioting in the camps and a protest on Wednesday from UNHCR Acting High Commissioner Sergio Vieira de Mello to Bangladesh Foreign Minister Abdus Samad Azad.
O'Toole said on Friday no formal reply had been received to that protest or earlier letters sent to Bangladesh authorities at the local level.
